BANK OF GHANA — CONSUMER PROTECTION IN BANKING (SUMMARY FOR SIKA AI)

The Bank of Ghana (BoG) is Ghana's central regulator for banks and specialised deposit-taking institutions (SDIs), operating under the Banks and Specialised Deposit-Taking Institutions Act, 2016 (Act 930). Under this Act, BoG is responsible for promoting the safety and soundness of banks and SDIs, ensuring the stability of the financial system, and developing consumer protection measures to protect the interests of bank and SDI customers.

In February 2017, BoG issued Consumer Recourse Mechanism Guidelines for Financial Service Providers. These apply to banks, non-bank financial institutions, specialised deposit-taking institutions, financial holding companies, and their affiliates regulated by BoG. The guidelines set ou

titutions, financial holding companies, and their affiliates regulated by BoG. The guidelines set out how customers can raise complaints, how providers must respond, and escalation paths if a complaint is not resolved to the customer's satisfaction, including the right to eventually seek redress through the courts.

BoG also runs an Investigation and Consumer Reporting Office (ICRO), which handles consumer protection matters and financial education.

Deposit protection: Ghana has a Deposit Protection Scheme created under the Ghana Deposit Protection Act (Act 931), managed by the Ghana Deposit Protection Corporation (GDPC). This scheme guarantees depositors compensation up to a set cedi amount if a bank or SDI fails — this is not automatic full protection of all deposits, only up to the sch

t if a bank or SDI fails — this is not automatic full protection of all deposits, only up to the scheme's covered limit, so customers should confirm the current coverage cap directly with GDPC or BoG since this figure is periodically reviewed.

For Sika AI: when discussing bank safety, deposit protection, or complaint escalation, note that BoG-regulated institutions have formal consumer recourse channels, but always recommend the customer verify current procedures and coverage limits with BoG (bog.gov.gh) or GDPC directly, since exact figures and procedures are updated periodically.

BUSINESS REGISTRATION IN GHANA — SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP (REGISTRAR GENERAL'S DEPARTMENT / OFFICE OF THE REGISTRAR OF COMPANIES)

Business registration in Ghana is handled through the Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC), operating under the Registrar-General's Department (RGD). The RGD was originally established in 1950 and has long been the government body responsible for registering companies and businesses.

Steps to register a sole proprietorship ("business name" / "one-man business"):

1. Choose a unique business name and conduct a name search at RGD (in person or via the RGD portal, rgd.gov.gh) to confirm no one else is using it.
2. Apply for a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) from the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) before registering the business — a copy of the Ghana Card is

rom the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) before registering the business — a copy of the Ghana Card is typically required for this. TIN issuance generally takes one to two days once submitted.
3. Complete the sole proprietorship registration form, known as Form A, available from RGD's website or offices. Required information typically includes: business name, business address (digital address, house/building details, street, city, district), postal address, email, phone number, and the residential address of the business owner.
4. Pay the applicable registration fee at an RGD-designated bank; you will receive an official receipt.
5. RGD issues a Certificate of Registration and a certified true copy of Form A once processing is complete. Registration commonly takes about 7 days, though expedit

copy of Form A once processing is complete. Registration commonly takes about 7 days, though expedited/"prestige" services may be available at some offices for faster turnaround.
6. Sole proprietorship business name registration must be renewed annually.

For registered companies (limited liability): additional requirements apply, including a proposed company name search, at least one director/shareholder, a registered office address, and company regulations/constitution documents. Company registration involves more documentation, higher fees (which vary based on authorised share capital), and may benefit from professional (legal/accounting) support.

Applications for both business types can generally be submitted online through the e-Registrar portal or in person at RGD/ORC offices.

Tax

generally be submitted online through the e-Registrar portal or in person at RGD/ORC offices.

Tax note: a sole proprietor and their sole proprietorship business are treated as one entity for tax purposes — the owner is personally liable for business debts, and business income is taxed as part of the owner's personal income.

For Sika AI: exact fees, forms, and turnaround times change over time and vary by office/urgency of service — always tell the user to confirm current fees and requirements directly with RGD (rgd.gov.gh) or GRA (gra.gov.gh) rather than quoting a specific fee as fixed.

GHANA DEPOSIT PROTECTION SCHEME (GDPC) — DEPOSIT INSURANCE

The Ghana Deposit Protection Corporation (GDPC) operates the national deposit insurance scheme under the Ghana Deposit Protection Act, 2016 (Act 931). It protects small depositors when a licensed bank or Specialized Deposit-Taking Institution (SDI) fails. The scheme launched in September 2019.

CURRENT COVERAGE LIMITS:
- Banks: maximum compensation of GHS 6,250 per depositor.
- Specialized Deposit-Taking Institutions (SDIs — savings and loans, microfinance companies, rural/community banks): maximum GHS 1,250 per depositor.

HOW IT WORKS:
- All deposit accounts a depositor holds with the failed institution are aggregated for the compensation calculation, and any overdue liabilities owed to that institution are deducted.
- Any amoun

ensation calculation, and any overdue liabilities owed to that institution are deducted.
- Any amount above the insured limit is NOT covered by the scheme; the depositor may claim the excess from the Receiver/Liquidator of the failed institution.
- Pay-outs begin about 6 days after the failure and must be completed within 30 days.
- The scheme protects small deposits; keeping more than the limit in a single institution leaves the excess at risk.

IMPORTANT UPDATE — UNDER REVIEW:
- The Ghana Deposit Protection (Amendment) Act, 2025 now requires the GDPC Board to review the coverage limits every two years to keep compensation in line with economic conditions. The Board began such a review in May 2026, so the GHS 6,250 / GHS 1,250 limits may change. Always confirm current limits at gdpc.gov.g

ay 2026, so the GHS 6,250 / GHS 1,250 limits may change. Always confirm current limits at gdpc.gov.gh before advising a user on how much is protected.

CONTEXT:
- The scheme was a response to the financial sector clean-up of 2017–2020, during which the government spent over GHS 21 billion compensating depositors of collapsed banks and other financial institutions.
- Deposit insurance is backed by a Deposit Protection Fund financed by premiums from member institutions, with initial seed funding from the Government of Ghana and the Bank of Ghana (with KfW technical support).

For Sika AI: reassure savers that deposits up to the limit are protected, but warn that money beyond the limit in one failed institution is not guaranteed. Advise spreading large balances across institutions and confirm

ailed institution is not guaranteed. Advise spreading large balances across institutions and confirming the current limit at gdpc.gov.gh. Note that treasury bills and other investments are NOT deposits and are not covered by the scheme.

ELECTRONIC TRANSFER LEVY (E-LEVY) — STATUS AND HISTORY

The Electronic Transfer Levy ("E-Levy"), introduced under the Electronic Transfer Levy Act, 2022 (Act 1075), was a tax on electronic money transfers in Ghana, covering mobile money transfers, bank transfers, merchant payments, and inward remittances. It was first proposed at 1.75% in the 2022 budget, reduced to 1.5% before implementation in May 2022 amid strong public opposition, and later reduced further to 1% from March 2023.

IMPORTANT UPDATE: The E-Levy was fully repealed. As part of the 2025 Budget Statement presented to Parliament on 11 March 2025 by Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, the government proposed abolishing the E-Levy (along with the betting tax and emissions levy) to ease the financial burden on households. Pa

-Levy (along with the betting tax and emissions levy) to ease the financial burden on households. Parliament passed the Electronic Transfer Levy (Repeal) Bill, 2025 on 26 March 2025, and President John Dramani Mahama signed it into law on 2 April 2025. The Electronic Transfer Levy (Repeal) Act, 2025 (Act 1128) repealed the original Act 1075 (and its amendment, Act 1089), effective 2 April 2025. GRA directed all charging entities (banks, mobile money providers, fintechs) to stop applying the 1% E-Levy charge by that date.

This means that, as of the repeal date, electronic mobile money transfers, bank transfers, and similar transactions are NO LONGER subject to the E-Levy in Ghana.

For Sika AI: this is a clear example of a policy that has changed since older training knowledge — if a user

AI: this is a clear example of a policy that has changed since older training knowledge — if a user asks about E-Levy, prioritize live search/RAG confirmation of current status over any older assumption that it's still active at 1% or 1.5%, since some outdated web content may still reference the levy as if it were in effect. Always note the date of the information you're citing, and recommend the user check gra.gov.gh for the latest confirmation if anything seems inconsistent.

GHANA FINANCIAL INCLUSION — CONTEXT AND STATISTICS

Ghana has made significant progress on formal financial inclusion. According to the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025, approximately 81% of Ghanaian adults had a financial account as of 2024 — among the highest rates in Sub-Saharan Africa, tied with South Africa and behind only Kenya and Mauritius regionally.

Ghana's Ministry of Finance also tracks a Composite Financial Inclusion Index (CFII) combining access, usage, and quality dimensions across roughly 40 indicators; this index rose from about 52.76% in 2022 to 56.60% in 2023, reflecting a moderate but improving overall level of financial inclusion — access to formal services is relatively widespread, but active usage and service quality still have room to grow.

Mobile money ha

elatively widespread, but active usage and service quality still have room to grow.

Mobile money has been the primary driver of this growth. Regionally, mobile money accounts for a large share of new financial inclusion — roughly a fifth of all adults in Sub-Saharan Africa have no financial account other than a mobile money wallet, making it many people's sole entry point into formal finance. In Ghana specifically, a large majority of adults who borrow any money do so through mobile-money-linked credit products rather than traditional bank loans — reflecting how central MoMo has become not just for payments, but for everyday informal credit access.

Ghana's National Financial Inclusion and Development Strategy (NFIDS 2018–2023) set a target of 85% of adults having a digital financial acco

Development Strategy (NFIDS 2018–2023) set a target of 85% of adults having a digital financial account by the end of 2023, structured around five pillars: financial stability, access/quality/usage of services, financial infrastructure, financial consumer protection, and financial capability. GhIPSS (the Bank of Ghana subsidiary managing mobile money interoperability, GhQR, and related systems) is one of the key infrastructure providers supporting this strategy.

Historical earlier data points (FinScope Ghana surveys) found that Ghanaians who save often prefer transactional and savings products over credit products — historically fewer Ghanaians used formal credit compared to those using savings or transactional accounts, suggesting many people are more comfortable saving formally than bor

ings or transactional accounts, suggesting many people are more comfortable saving formally than borrowing formally, which is relevant context when discussing savings versus credit options with users.

For Sika AI: use these figures as general context on how mainstream mobile money and formal accounts have become in Ghana, while still respecting that a meaningful share of users (especially older, rural, or lower-income Ghanaians) may still rely partly or fully on cash and informal mechanisms like susu. Always frame formal financial inclusion progress evenhandedly rather than implying informal tools are obsolete.

GRA MODIFIED TAXATION SCHEME (MTS) — INFORMAL SECTOR TAXATION

The Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) operates a Modified Taxation Scheme (MTS), a simplified form of Personal Income Tax designed for people working in the informal sector — including artisans, traders, hairdressers, seamstresses, mechanics, food vendors, and similar small-scale operators. GRA describes this as a "pay-as-you-go" digital approach that replaces complex traditional tax assessments with simplified registration and payment tools.

The MTS has three main categories:

1. Presumptive Tax Based on Instalment (PTI) — fixed tax amounts based on income level and business activity, generally for businesses with average annual turnover not exceeding GHS 20,000 over three consecutive years (one or two years of data can be used i

rnover not exceeding GHS 20,000 over three consecutive years (one or two years of data can be used if three years isn't available).

2. Presumptive Tax Based on Turnover (PTT) — a flat rate of 3% applied to annual turnover, generally for businesses with turnover above GHS 20,000 but not exceeding GHS 500,000.

3. Modified Cash Basis (MCB) — tax calculated on earnings after deducting expenses related to those earnings, typically for slightly larger informal operations.

To qualify for PTI or PTT, a person must earn income only from sources within Ghana and must not be registered for VAT. The following CANNOT use PTI or PTT and must instead use MCB or standard taxation: professionals with formal qualifications (e.g. lawyers, engineers, accountants), owners of multiple businesses or outlets,

al qualifications (e.g. lawyers, engineers, accountants), owners of multiple businesses or outlets, partners in formally registered business partnerships, and anyone who voluntarily opts out of presumptive tax.

GRA also operates a Small Taxpayer Office (STO) network — around 50 offices nationwide — as a one-stop shop for small/informal taxpayers to handle domestic tax transactions. Small taxpayers are presumed to operate informally and generally not keep full business records. GRA also issues a Tax Stamp — a specially designed stamp given to small-scale informal businesses as evidence of having paid their taxes.

IMPORTANT (2026 UPDATE): The VAT Flat Rate Scheme (VFRS) that previously applied to many small taxpayers was ABOLISHED effective 1 January 2026 by the Value Added Tax Act, 2025 (

ed to many small taxpayers was ABOLISHED effective 1 January 2026 by the Value Added Tax Act, 2025 (Act 1151). VAT-registered small taxpayers must now charge VAT at the standard rate (15% VAT + 2.5% NHIL + 2.5% GETFund = 20% effective), and the VAT registration threshold rose from GHS 200,000 to GHS 750,000. See the vat_act_2026_reform document for details.

Context: Ghana's informal sector makes up roughly 80% of the country's workforce (Ghana Statistical Service, 2023) but contributes only around 30% of GDP, a gap attributed to complex tax processes, low tax morale, and limited tax awareness — which is part of why GRA introduced MTS.

For Sika AI: use this to explain likely tax categories to informal workers, but always tell the user that current turnover thresholds, rates, and STO locat

to informal workers, but always tell the user that current turnover thresholds, rates, and STO locations should be confirmed with GRA (gra.gov.gh) directly, since GRA periodically updates thresholds through annual budget statements.

GHANA PERSONAL INCOME TAX — PAYE BANDS AND SELF-EMPLOYMENT

Personal income tax in Ghana is progressive: each band rate applies only to the slice of chargeable income within that band, not the whole amount. The current bands were set by the Income Tax (Amendment) (No. 2) Act, 2023 (Act 1111) and took effect 1 January 2024. They remain the applicable bands (confirmed by GRA through 2026).

MONTHLY RESIDENT BANDS (Act 1111):
- First GHS 490/month: 0%
- Next GHS 110 (490–600): 5%
- Next GHS 130 (600–730): 10%
- Next GHS 3,166.67 (730–3,896.67): 17.5%
- Next GHS 16,000 (3,896.67–19,896.67): 25%
- Next GHS 30,520 (19,896.67–50,416.67): 30%
- Above GHS 50,416.67/month: 35%

ANNUAL EQUIVALENTS:
- First GHS 5,880/year: 0%
- Next GHS 1,320 (5,880–7,200): 5%
- Next GHS 1,560 (7,200–8,760): 10%
- Nex

irst GHS 5,880/year: 0%
- Next GHS 1,320 (5,880–7,200): 5%
- Next GHS 1,560 (7,200–8,760): 10%
- Next GHS 38,000 (8,760–46,760): 17.5%
- Next GHS 192,000 (46,760–238,760): 25%
- Next GHS 366,240 (238,760–605,000): 30%
- Above GHS 605,000/year: 35%

OTHER KEY FACTS:
- Chargeable income is total income (employment, business, investment) less allowable deductions/reliefs. Employment income (PAYE) is deducted and remitted monthly by the employer on or before the 15th day of the following month.
- Non-resident individuals are generally taxed at a flat rate of 25% of chargeable income.
- Anyone earning above GHS 490/month as an employee is liable to personal income tax.
- Self-employed people and informal workers may instead fall under the GRA Modified Taxation Scheme (presumptive tax based on i

informal workers may instead fall under the GRA Modified Taxation Scheme (presumptive tax based on instalment or turnover, or modified cash basis) — see the MTS document. Those earning income only from within Ghana and not VAT-registered can qualify for presumptive tax. Formally qualified professionals (lawyers, engineers, accountants), owners of multiple businesses, and partners in registered partnerships cannot use presumptive tax.
- SSNIT pension contributions and Tier 3 voluntary contributions are tax-relieved subject to limits.
- Tax on interest from Government of Ghana securities (treasury bills/notes/bonds) is generally exempt for resident individuals.

For Sika AI: use the monthly bands to walk a user through what they will pay on a given salary. Give a concrete worked example. Alw

nds to walk a user through what they will pay on a given salary. Give a concrete worked example. Always advise confirming with GRA (gra.gov.gh) or a tax practitioner because bands and thresholds change through annual budget statements (e.g., Act 1111 updated the old 2020 bands).

INSURANCE IN GHANA — LICENSING, COMPULSORY MOTOR COVER, AND MICRO-INSURANCE

The insurance industry in Ghana is regulated by the National Insurance Commission (NIC) under the Insurance Act, 2021 (Act 1061), which replaced the old 2006 Act. Act 1061 modernized the sector — it separates life and non-life business, requires NIC approval of new products, and gives legal backing to micro-insurance.

KEY FACTS:
1. Licensing: All insurers must be licensed by the NIC. Insurers must be either life or non-life (composite companies were split up). Products must be NIC-approved to protect policyholders and ensure financial viability.
2. Compulsory motor insurance: Under the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958 (as amended), anyone who uses a vehicle on a public road MUST have motor third-p

nsurance) Act, 1958 (as amended), anyone who uses a vehicle on a public road MUST have motor third-party insurance. Options are:
   - Third Party (covers injury/death/damage to others only) — the most common and legally required minimum
   - Third Party, Fire & Theft (adds cover for fire/theft loss of your own vehicle)
   - Comprehensive (covers own damage plus third-party liabilities)
   The NIC also runs a Motor Insurance Compensation Fund that compensates road-accident victims who cannot recover from an insurer.
3. Micro-insurance: Section 209 of Act 1061 gives legal backing to micro-insurance sold through licensed channels (agents, mobile-money platforms, telecoms). Products are simplified, low-premium covers aimed at low-income customers — examples include mobile health/life cover (e.

ed, low-premium covers aimed at low-income customers — examples include mobile health/life cover (e.g., MTN aYo-type products), funeral policies, and credit-life bundled with loans. The Microinsurance Market Conduct Rules 2013 govern conduct.
4. Common products in Ghana: Whole life, term life (funeral, mortgage, credit life, keyman), endowment/wealth products, motor, fire/theft/property, accident, marine, liability, and micro-insurance covers. Life insurers must pay claims and face NIC solvency oversight.
5. Insurance penetration is low (around 1% of GDP), so many Ghanaians rely on informal risk-sharing (susu, funeral associations). Formal insurance can be a better fit for larger, harder risks.

BUYING INSURANCE — GOOD PRACTICE:
- Only buy from an NIC-licensed insurer; check nicgh.org if u

ks.

BUYING INSURANCE — GOOD PRACTICE:
- Only buy from an NIC-licensed insurer; check nicgh.org if unsure.
- Read what is covered and what is excluded; ask about premiums, waiting periods, and claims process before paying.
- For motor insurance, do not drive uninsured — it is illegal and third-party claims can be financially ruinous.
- For low-income users, ask about micro-insurance products sold via mobile money rather than assuming traditional premiums are out of reach.

For Sika AI: when a user asks about insurance, determine the type (life, motor, health, micro) and recommend verifying the insurer is NIC-licensed. Mention that motor third-party cover is compulsory by law. Do not recommend a specific insurer by name unless the user asks. Advise confirming current minimum premium rates a
d a specific insurer by name unless the user asks. Advise confirming current minimum premium rates and product details with the insurer or NIC (nicgh.org).

INVESTING IN GHANA — TREASURY BILLS, NOTES AND BONDS

Treasury bills are short-term Government of Ghana securities issued through weekly auctions run by the Bank of Ghana. They are considered low-risk ("risk-free" in the sense of being backed by government) and are a common first investment for Ghanaians. Returns are known at purchase, which makes them predictable but modest.

TYPES OF INSTRUMENT:
- 91-day Treasury Bill (3 months)
- 182-day Treasury Bill (6 months)
- 364-day Treasury Bill (1 year)
- 1- and 2-year Treasury Notes; 3- and 5-year Treasury Bonds (longer tenors, sold less frequently)

HOW IT WORKS:
- Bills are sold at a discount: you pay less than face value and receive the full face value at maturity. The difference is your return.
- Interest on Government of Ghana securities i

ace value at maturity. The difference is your return.
- Interest on Government of Ghana securities is generally EXEMPT from tax for resident individuals.
- Rates are set at weekly auctions and change constantly. Indicative auction results (Bank of Ghana, early August 2026): 91-day bill approx. 5.76%, 182-day approx. 7.64%, 364-day approx. 12.98%. These are illustrative only — always check the latest BoG auction result (bog.gov.gh) or your bank's current quote before acting.

HOW TO BUY:
- Bank branches (e.g., GCB, Ecobank, Stanbic, etc.) — minimum typically around GHS 500, needs valid photo ID (Ghana Card recommended) and a bank account.
- Bank mobile apps — requires a CSD (Central Securities Depository) account registered first at a branch.
- Brokers/investment houses (e.g., Databank) — m

s Depository) account registered first at a branch.
- Brokers/investment houses (e.g., Databank) — minimum approx. GHS 500; two passport photos + valid ID.
- Mobile money (e.g., Ecobank TBILL4ALL on MTN MoMo) — from as little as GHS 5 for 91/182-day bills, full payout to your MoMo wallet at maturity, with optional automatic reinvestment.
- BoG's official direct minimum is GHS 100, but individual banks/brokers set their own higher practical minimums — ask before planning around a floor.

TIPS:
- Longer tenors generally pay higher rates, but rates reset every auction and your money is locked for the term.
- A ladder (splitting across 91/182/364-day bills) gives regular maturities and liquidity.
- Set a standing instruction to auto-roll matured bills into the next auction to avoid idle cash.

.
- Set a standing instruction to auto-roll matured bills into the next auction to avoid idle cash.
- Treasury bills can also be used as collateral and their statements help with visa applications.

RISKS AND LIMITS:
- Purchasing power risk: if inflation exceeds your return, real returns can be negative. Compare against the current inflation rate.
- These are savings-grade investments, not high-growth investments. They are not bank deposits and are not covered by deposit insurance (GDPC) — though as government securities the default risk is considered very low.
- Money needed before maturity is locked in; early exit usually means selling on the secondary market, often at a discount.

For Sika AI: when discussing investing, distinguish risk profiles — T-bills for low-risk savers, and note t

a AI: when discussing investing, distinguish risk profiles — T-bills for low-risk savers, and note that returns depend on the latest BoG auction (always pull current rates via the live data tool or web search rather than quoting from memory). Also compare T-bill returns with the current inflation rate before recommending. Direct users to bog.gov.gh/treasury-bill-rates for the official weekly auction results.

LOANS AND CREDIT IN GHANA — BANKS, MOBILE MONEY LOANS, AND CREDIT REPORTING

Borrowing in Ghana ranges from informal (susu groups, family) to formal (banks, microfinance/SDIs) to digital (mobile-money loans). Digital lending has exploded because it needs no collateral or paperwork — but it is often expensive.

MOBILE MONEY / DIGITAL LOANS:
- MTN Qwik Loan (MTN MoMo, powered by Letshego Ghana) — borrow from as little as GHS 1 up to roughly GHS 1,000–2,000, repaid in 24 hours to 90 days. Pricing is high: roughly 9% for a 24-hour loan, a flat ~6.9% fee on the 30-day product, rising sharply for longer tenures (up to ~30% for 90 days). Approving/rejecting depends on MoMo activity (wallet age ~90+ days, monthly transaction volume, airtime spend) and credit history.
- Other digital lenders: Branc

days, monthly transaction volume, airtime spend) and credit history.
- Other digital lenders: Branch, Fido, OKash, Hubtel Lend, AirtelTigo Money Boost, Telecel Cash Advance. Limits typically grow from small starter loans (GHS 50–200) as you repay on time.
- These loans are automatically repaid by deduction from your MoMo wallet; keep funds available on the due date.

COST WARNING:
- Short tenures + flat fees can translate to very high effective annual rates. Mobile loans are best used as short-term bridging, not long-term borrowing. Borrow only what you can repay within the term.

CREDIT REPORTING AND YOUR SCORE:
- Ghana has licensed credit bureaus: XDS Data (formerly CreditInfo Ghana) and Dun & Bradstreet Ghana, regulated by the Bank of Ghana under the Credit Reporting Act, 2007 (Act 750

Dun & Bradstreet Ghana, regulated by the Bank of Ghana under the Credit Reporting Act, 2007 (Act 750).
- Lenders (banks, fintechs, telcos) report and check records. Defaults are shared across lenders via the bureaus and can block you from future credit (bank loans, credit cards, other apps) and affect some background checks.
- On-time repayment builds a positive file; missing payments damages it (defaults can follow you for years). You can request your credit report from a bureau (usually for a small fee, e.g., around GHS 20) to check and correct errors.
- The Ghana Card is increasingly central: identity-linked credit means you cannot escape obligations by changing SIMs or numbers.
- No single national FICO-style score exists — each lender scores differently — but shared default data matte

le national FICO-style score exists — each lender scores differently — but shared default data matters everywhere.

BANK LOANS:
- Banks generally require: a valid Ghana Card, income proof/employment history or business records, and often a guarantor or collateral for larger loans. Interest is usually quoted annually (e.g., flat or reducing-balance) — always ask whether the rate is reducing balance or flat rate, because the true cost differs dramatically (see calculate-loan-payment skill).
- Building a documented banking/MoMo history supports future loan approvals.

GOOD PRACTICE FOR BORROWERS:
1. Borrow only for something that improves your situation, and only what you can repay.
2. Compare the true cost: ask for the annual effective rate, not just the daily/flat fee.
3. Never borrow to ga

the true cost: ask for the annual effective rate, not just the daily/flat fee.
3. Never borrow to gamble, and avoid loan apps with hidden fees or aggressive collection.
4. Repay on time — it protects your credit file and grows your limits.
5. If an app pressures you into a loan you don't understand, walk away; legitimate lenders disclose terms clearly.

For Sika AI: when a user asks about taking a loan, first establish purpose and repayment capacity. If a mobile-money loan is proposed, convert the fee to an annualized cost and warn if it is very high. Explain that defaults hit their credit bureau file and future access to credit. Mention the option of a formal bank loan for larger needs and that building repayment history helps. Do not recommend a specific lender by name unless asked.

MICROFINANCE INSTITUTION TIERS IN GHANA (INCLUDING 2026 REGULATORY REFORM)

Historically (since a 2011 Bank of Ghana framework), microfinance institutions in Ghana were classified into four tiers based on the type of activity they carried out:

- Tier 1: Rural and Community Banks (RCBs), Finance Houses, and Savings & Loans Companies (S&Ls) — regulated under the Banking Act.
- Tier 2: Deposit-taking Microfinance Companies (MFCs) — licensed and supervised by BoG's Other Financial Institutions Supervision Department (OFISD).
- Tier 3: Micro-Credit Companies (money lenders, "susu" companies operating as credit-only) and Financial NGOs (FNGOs) — generally credit-only, not permitted to take deposits from the general public in the same way as Tiers 1–2.
- Tier 4: Individual susu collectors and ot

ts from the general public in the same way as Tiers 1–2.
- Tier 4: Individual susu collectors and other informal, non-deposit-taking operators, historically expected to eventually formalize under an apex body (e.g. the Ghana Cooperative Susu Collectors Association).

Credit unions are a related but separately regulated category, supervised under the Co-operative Credit Union Regulations (overseen historically in coordination with the Ghana Co-operative Credit Unions Association, CUA).

IMPORTANT UPDATE — 2026 reform: Bank of Ghana has introduced a new regulatory framework replacing the old four-tier, activity-based structure with a revised set of institutional categories defined primarily by institutional form, capital thresholds, ownership, and governance requirements, rather than simply

institutional form, capital thresholds, ownership, and governance requirements, rather than simply by the type of activity performed. Under the new framework:
- A new "Microfinance Bank (MFB)" category is being introduced as a licensed deposit-taking institution primarily serving small businesses, informal groups, and individual clients, with a substantially higher minimum capital requirement (reported around GHS 50 million for existing institutions transitioning in, and GHS 100 million for new entrants).
- A new "Community Bank (CB)" category is set to replace the old Rural Bank designation, serving both rural and urban communities with a community-focused deposit-taking model.
- Existing Savings and Loans Companies, Finance Houses, Deposit-taking Microfinance Companies, and Micro-Credit

Savings and Loans Companies, Finance Houses, Deposit-taking Microfinance Companies, and Micro-Credit Companies may transition into the new MFB category if they meet BoG's requirements.
- All existing institutions are required to transition into one of the new categories by 31 December 2026.

This is a live regulatory transition — detailed governance and operational directives were still being issued by BoG as of the reform announcement.

Other regulators in Ghana's financial sector: the National Insurance Commission (NIC) regulates insurance (including micro-insurance products aimed at informal-sector customers), the National Pensions Regulatory Authority (NPRA) regulates private pension schemes (Tier 2/Tier 3 of the pension system), and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana r

emes (Tier 2/Tier 3 of the pension system), and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana regulates capital markets operators, investment products, and fund managers.

For Sika AI: because this reform is actively in transition through the end of 2026, always flag to users that MFI tier names and capital categories are changing, and recommend confirming an institution's current licensing status directly with Bank of Ghana (bog.gov.gh) — especially before trusting a lender or savings collector claiming a specific tier/license.

MOBILE MONEY, GHIPSS, AND GHANA'S PAYMENT INFRASTRUCTURE

Ghana Interbank Payment and Settlement Systems Limited (GhIPSS) is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Bank of Ghana, incorporated in 2007, mandated to build and manage interoperable electronic payment infrastructure for banks and non-bank financial institutions across the country.

Key GhIPSS-run payment systems:

1. Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI) — launched May 2018. Allows users to transfer funds directly between mobile wallets on DIFFERENT networks (e.g., MTN MoMo to Telecel Cash), and between mobile wallets and bank accounts or e-zwich cards. To use it, a customer typically dials their existing mobile money short code and follows the prompts, or contacts their mobile money provider for guidance — no separate app or registrati

ws the prompts, or contacts their mobile money provider for guidance — no separate app or registration is required beyond an active mobile money wallet.

2. GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP) — a real-time, account-to-account transfer system accessible via mobile, internet banking, ATM, or POS, enabling near-instant transfers between different banks.

3. GhQR — Ghana's universal QR code payment system, allowing a single QR code standard to work across multiple banks, mobile money wallets, and payment cards, simplifying merchant payment acceptance.

4. gh-link — Ghana's domestic EMV card scheme, a locally processed alternative to international card networks (Visa/Mastercard), intended to reduce transaction costs and keep transaction value within Ghana.

5. e-zwich — Ghana's national biometric smart c

tion costs and keep transaction value within Ghana.

5. e-zwich — Ghana's national biometric smart card and switch system linking payment platforms of licensed banks and non-bank financial institutions.

6. GhanaPay — a bank-led mobile money product (distinct from telco-led MoMo services) that integrates with banking services, offering account holders access to savings, bill payments, and in some cases interest on wallet balances.

Regulatory context: all of these systems operate under Bank of Ghana oversight via GhIPSS. Ghana's National Financial Inclusion and Development Strategy has explicitly promoted mobile money interoperability and digital payment infrastructure as core tools for expanding financial access, particularly for informal-sector and rural populations who may lack easy acc

Financial inclusion snapshot: Ghana's account ownership rate reached approximately 81% of adults as of 2024 (World Bank Global Findex 2025), among the highest in Sub-Saharan Africa, with mobile money identified as the primary driver of this growth — in the region generally, roughly 20% of adults have no financial account other than a mobile money wallet, meaning mobile money is often someone's only entry point into the formal financial system. In Ghana specifically, a large majority of formal borrowers who take any loan borrow through mobile money providers rather than banks, reflecting how central MoMo-linked credit products have become for everyday borrow

ather than banks, reflecting how central MoMo-linked credit products have become for everyday borrowing.

It provides financial coverage for basic healthcare services and covers an estimated 95%+ of common disease conditions seen at Ghanaian health facilities, including general outpatient/inpatient care, maternal care (including caesarean delivery), and a list of NHIA-approved essential drugs. Some services are excluded, such as dialysis for chronic renal failure, most cancer treatments (aside from cervical and breast cancer), organ transplants, and cosmetic procedures.

PERSONAL FINANCE FOUNDATIONS FOR GHANAIAN HOUSEHOLDS

Practical money-management basics, adapted to the realities of the Ghanaian economy: irregular income, a mix of cash and mobile money, large family obligations, and limited access to formal credit. These are general principles, not binding rules.

BUDGETING WITH IRREGULAR OR SEASONAL INCOME:
- When income varies (traders, farmers, drivers, artisans), do not budget from last month's peak. Use a "base income" — your most reliable, lowest realistic monthly income — and treat anything above it as surplus.
- Divide money into four buckets and decide shares up front:
  1. Essentials: rent, food, transport, school fees, health.
  2. Savings & investment: fixed amount or share of every sale — pay yourself first.
  3. Debt repayment: if you have

vestment: fixed amount or share of every sale — pay yourself first.
  3. Debt repayment: if you have loans, clear the most expensive first.
  4. Optional/fun: whatever remains.
- Use a simple tracker (notebook or a mobile wallet statement) so money doesn't silently disappear.
- During good months, pre-fund future essentials (buy staple food in bulk, top up school fees) to smooth bad months.

EMERGENCY FUND:
- Aim to build an emergency buffer equal to 1–3 months of essential expenses before taking on non-essential debt or investing.
- Keep it accessible: a dedicated mobile-money wallet or savings account that you don't touch except for real emergencies.
- Do not invest money you might need quickly in locked instruments (e.g., 364-day treasury bills) unless you can afford the lock-up.

SAVING AND INVESTING:
- Savings should earn something. Compare: susu (convenient, group discipline, but usually no interest), MoMo goal savings (some pay interest), bank fixed deposits, treasury bills, and credit-union savings. See the compare-savings-options skill.
- Only consider investments (stocks, bonds, funds) for money you can leave untouched for 1–3 years.
- If an offer promises "guaranteed" high returns, it is almost certainly a scam. Verify any institution with its regulator (BoG, SEC, NIC).

DEBT DISCIPLINE:
- A common safe guideline: total monthly debt payments should stay well below half of your base income.
- Never borrow to gamble or to buy things that lose value on credit at very

- Never borrow to gamble or to buy things that lose value on credit at very high cost.
- If you are struggling, talk to the lender early — negotiating beats defaulting, which damages your credit file (see loans document).

FAMILY AND COMMUNITY MONEY:
- Set clear expectations with family/friends about what you can contribute — many Ghanaians over-give and under-save.
- Community savings (susu, VSLA, rotating groups) work best as discipline tools and emergency pools, not as the primary home for large savings.
- Protect against big shocks with insurance where cheap (e.g., NHIS, micro-insurance, compulsory motor third-party) rather than only relying on friends.

COMMON FINANCIAL SCAM PATTERNS AFFECTING GHANAIANS (PROTECTIVE OVERVIEW)

Ghanaian consumers, particularly mobile money users, have been targeted by a range of fraud patterns reported by Bank of Ghana, telco fraud desks, and consumer protection sources. This document summarizes general categories and protective responses — not operational detail — for use in user-facing guidance.

General categories of reported fraud:
- Impersonation of trusted institutions or people: fraudsters posing as telco customer care, bank staff, government officials, or even cloned voices of family members, typically creating urgency or fear to prompt quick action.
- Unauthorized SIM reissuance: criminals gaining control of a victim's phone number through fraudulent means, which can then be used to intercept codes

ntrol of a victim's phone number through fraudulent means, which can then be used to intercept codes tied to a mobile money account.
- Fake investment or job schemes: offers of unusually high, guaranteed, low-risk returns, or job opportunities that require an upfront "registration" or "processing" payment before anything is delivered.
- Romance-based fraud: relationships built over messaging platforms that escalate into requests for money, often for a fabricated emergency.
- Money mule recruitment: being asked to receive transfers into your own mobile money account and forward them elsewhere for a fee — this can carry serious legal risk to the account holder, since Ghana's Anti-Money Laundering Act framework can implicate the receiving account holder, and accounts used this way risk being

ing Act framework can implicate the receiving account holder, and accounts used this way risk being frozen by Bank of Ghana.
- Fake agent scams: unlicensed or unofficial mobile money agent setups designed to intercept transaction details or PINs during ordinary cash transactions.

Shared red flags across these patterns: any request for a PIN, OTP (one-time password), or full account/Ghana Card details over a phone call or message; pressure to act immediately or to keep an opportunity secret from family; guaranteed high returns with no real risk explained; and unsolicited contact claiming to be from a bank, telco, or government body asking to "verify" sensitive details.

Protective actions:
- Never share a MoMo PIN or OTP with anyone — legitimate telcos, banks, and government agencies do no

Never share a MoMo PIN or OTP with anyone — legitimate telcos, banks, and government agencies do not ask for these over a call or message.
- If contacted by someone claiming to represent an institution, hang up and call that institution back using its official published number, rather than any number the caller provides.
- Verify unexpected requests for money — including from someone who sounds like a known contact — through a separate, trusted channel before acting.
- Report suspected fraud promptly: to the mobile network's official fraud/customer care line, to Bank of Ghana, and where relevant to Ghana's Cyber Security Authority or the police. Faster reporting improves the chance of freezing funds before they are moved further.
- Be cautious about agreeing to receive and forward funds f

ing funds before they are moved further.
- Be cautious about agreeing to receive and forward funds for someone else, even for a fee — this can carry legal risk regardless of whether the account holder realized the money was linked to fraud.

Relevant legal context: Ghana's Cybercrime Act (Act 1038) covers computer and identity fraud offences, and Ghana's Anti-Money Laundering Act framework covers the movement of illicit funds through accounts, including via money mule arrangements.

GHANA'S THREE-TIER PENSION SYSTEM (SSNIT / NPRA)

Ghana's pension system, established under the National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), has three tiers:

Tier 1 — Basic National Social Security Scheme (mandatory): A defined-benefit scheme managed by the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT). Formal-sector employees contribute a mandatory percentage of basic salary; contributions are tax-exempt and pay monthly pensions upon retirement, plus survivor and invalidity benefits. Of the total mandatory contribution, a portion is also channeled to NHIS to help fund national health insurance.

Tier 2 — Mandatory Occupational Pension Scheme: A mandatory defined-contribution scheme, NOT managed by SSNIT but by NPRA-licensed private trustees. Pays a lump sum at retirement based on total

anaged by SSNIT but by NPRA-licensed private trustees. Pays a lump sum at retirement based on total contributions plus investment returns.

Tier 3 — Voluntary Provident Fund / Personal Pension Scheme: A voluntary, privately managed defined-contribution scheme open to formal sector workers AND informal-sector/self-employed workers. Contributions of up to 16.5% of basic salary (for employees) are tax-deductible/tax-exempt. If a contributor stays in the scheme 10 years or more, they receive all contributions plus investment returns at exit. Exiting before the 10-year mark triggers a 15% marginal tax rate on the redemption amount. Early access before retirement is also possible after 5 years of contributions for informal-sector schemes (10 years for formal-sector schemes), or in cases of certi

contributions for informal-sector schemes (10 years for formal-sector schemes), or in cases of certified permanent incapacity or death (paid to beneficiaries/estate).

Self-Employed Enrolment Drive (SEED): SSNIT runs a specific initiative (SEED) to enroll self-employed persons and informal-sector workers into the Tier 1 scheme, allowing them to contribute voluntarily on their full earnings for old-age and invalidity protection. Any self-employed worker aged 15–45 who has never been a SSNIT member can register; people who were formerly formally employed can also reactivate a dormant SSNIT account regardless of age.

The National Pensions Regulatory Authority (NPRA) regulates and oversees all private and public pension activity, including Tier 2 and Tier 3 schemes and their licensed trustees

private and public pension activity, including Tier 2 and Tier 3 schemes and their licensed trustees.

For Sika AI: use this to explain pension options for informal workers (especially SEED and Tier 3 voluntary schemes), but recommend the user confirm current contribution rates, minimum enrollment ages, and procedures directly with SSNIT (ssnit.org.gh) or NPRA (npra.gov.gh), since specific administrative details can change.

SUSU AND INFORMAL SAVINGS SYSTEMS IN GHANA

Susu is a long-standing informal savings practice in Ghana, believed to derive from an Akan term related to "small small" or planned saving — the principle of saving small amounts regularly to build up a meaningful sum over time. It is one of the most widely used micro-savings mechanisms in Ghana, particularly among low- and middle-income earners, and is especially popular among market women and other informal traders.

Main forms of susu and related informal savings groups:
1. Susu Collectors — individuals (sometimes called "susu men/women") who visit clients daily at their workplace to collect a fixed contribution. At the end of an agreed period (commonly a month), the saver receives back their accumulated deposits, typically minus one day's co

(commonly a month), the saver receives back their accumulated deposits, typically minus one day's contribution as the collector's commission.
2. Rotating Savings and Credit Associations (ROSCAs) — groups where members contribute a fixed amount into a shared pool, which is then given in full to a different member each cycle in rotation.
3. Accumulating Savings and Credit Associations (ASCRAs) — groups where contributions build up a shared fund used for larger lump-sum needs, such as funerals or ceremonies.
4. Susu Companies — more formalized, registered entities that, beyond collecting savings, may extend loans to clients after a minimum saving history has been established.

Regulation: Bank of Ghana has, since 2011, worked to bring susu companies under a clearer regulatory framework, disti

of Ghana has, since 2011, worked to bring susu companies under a clearer regulatory framework, distinguishing more formal, registered susu companies from informal individual collectors who operate largely on trust and social/community accountability rather than formal licensing. This means the safety and reliability of susu savings can vary significantly depending on whether the collector or company is registered/regulated.

Why susu persists alongside mobile money: susu requires no bank account, no formal identification, and no minimum balance, making it highly accessible. Behavioral-economics research describes the daily in-person collection as a "commitment device" — because a collector's visit creates a social obligation that is harder to break than an abstract personal savings goal, s

visit creates a social obligation that is harder to break than an abstract personal savings goal, savers using susu can maintain more consistent saving discipline than they might with a mobile money wallet, where funds are easy to withdraw and spend on impulse. Group-based susu/ROSCA participation also creates social accountability: missing a contribution affects a member's standing within their community group, which tends to reduce default rates.

Broader context: informal financial agents in Ghana also include moneylenders, traders/input distributors who extend informal credit, and family/community lending networks. In some parts of the country (particularly northern Ghana), the ratio of people to formal bank branches is far higher than the national average, which increases reliance on

people to formal bank branches is far higher than the national average, which increases reliance on informal savings mechanisms like susu.

GHANA VAT REFORM 2026 — VALUE ADDED TAX ACT, 2025 (ACT 1151)

The Value Added Tax Act, 2025 (Act 1151) took effect on 1 January 2026 and overhauled Ghana's VAT system. This is a major change from the pre-2026 rules and should be treated as the current position.

WHAT CHANGED:
1. VAT Flat Rate Scheme (VFRS) ABOLISHED. The former 3% flat rate on supplies of goods and the former 5% flat rate on certain supplies of immovable property were removed effective 1 January 2026. Businesses that used the flat rate (mainly wholesalers and retailers of goods) must now charge VAT at the standard rate.
2. Unified standard rate: VAT 15% + NHIL 2.5% + GETFund 2.5% = effective total rate of 20% on the same taxable value. (The pre-2026 effective rate was 21.9%.)
3. VAT registration threshold increased from GH

able value. (The pre-2026 effective rate was 21.9%.)
3. VAT registration threshold increased from GHS 200,000 to GHS 750,000 in annual taxable turnover.
4. Input tax credit: businesses on the standard scheme can claim input VAT, subject to the rules in Act 1151 and GRA VAT administrative guidelines.
5. Scope expanded to expressly include exploration of natural resources and export of non-traditional products (except cocoa, coffee, shea butter).
6. Zero-rating on locally manufactured textiles extended to December 2028.
7. Stricter penalties for failure to register for VAT.
